correctness.rationale: The Hilbert-component intersection \(D=C'\cap S\) has dimension \(7\): the dense incident-line locus has \(3\) parameters for the intersection point and \(4\) for an unordered pair of distinct lines through it; the planar-double-line locus has dimension at most \(6\). The published pair-space component \(\mathcal P_2\) is irreducible of dimension \(11\) and maps properly and dominantly to the \(8\)-fold \(S\), so \(Z=\mathcal P_1\cap\mathcal P_2=(\Gamma|_{\mathcal P_2})^{-1}(D)\) is a proper closed subset of dimension at most \(10\), while the fibre-dimension theorem gives a component of dimension at least \(7+(11-8)=10\). Hence \(\dim Z=10\). The projective-space fibres of \(\Psi\) show \(\Psi(Z)=\overline{\mathcal R}\cap T\). A general point over the incident-line locus is nonplanar, so Proposition 3.9 gives \(h^0(E(1))=1\) and \(\Psi\) is generically injective there, preserving dimension.

value.rationale: The dimension is one of two questions explicitly singled out by the initiating paper immediately after its boundary classification. The value \(10\) shows that the \(11\)-dimensional reflexive component meets the \(15\)-dimensional \(T\)-component along a divisor, providing a concrete geometric constraint on the boundary of a classical low-Chern-class sheaf moduli space. It is a natural structural invariant of the whole component intersection, not a selected finite slice or routine numerical example.
